title: quality
text:
Some documents in a store are noise: they match many queries and answer none. A scraped cookie banner, a navigation menu or a licence footer shows up in search results because its words are common, and it pushes real answers down the list. This module gives every document a noise score so you can find such documents and decide whether to remove them.
The score needs no labelled examples, no extra model and no second pass over the source files. It is computed from the chunk vectors and texts the store already holds. A cookie banner gives itself away in several ways at once: near-identical copies of it appear on many pages, its vector sits away from most of the corpus, and its words are ones that occur everywhere.
The default weights were measured in vishalakshi (evals/noise.py and evals/RESULTS.md in that repository) on three test corpora with boilerplate documents planted in them. The weighted score separated boilerplate from real documents with a mean AUC of 0.988 (0.967 to 1.000). AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen noise document scores above a randomly chosen real one, so 0.5 is a coin toss and 1.0 is perfect.
The functions read a tree store, the kind Index and add_doc build, because they need each chunk’s doc_id and the docs table for titles. A plain get_store table has neither.

chunk_matrix reads every chunk that has an embedding and returns its id, its document id, its text and its vector, with the vectors stacked into one float32 array and scaled to unit length. With unit vectors, a dot product is the cosine similarity. Pass limit to work on a random sample of chunks in a large store, and dtype if the store holds vectors in a width other than float16.

title: quality
section: Nearest neighbours, centroids and word rarity
text:
Nearest neighbours, centroids and word rarity
These helpers compute the quantities the features are built from. _knn finds each chunk’s nearest other chunks: exactly, by matrix product, up to 30,000 chunks, and through a temporary HNSW index above that, unless usearch’s HNSW index failed its probe. _centroids finds topic centres with k-means. chunk_idf splits text into words with TOKEN_RE and scores how rare each word is across chunks: inverse document frequency (IDF) is high for a word few chunks use and near zero for a word in nearly every chunk. _entropy measures how evenly a row of probabilities is spread, from 0 (all on one value) to 1 (spread evenly).

text:
The features
noise_features computes nine numbers per document. Each is computed per chunk and averaged over the document’s chunks, and in each a larger value means more likely noise.

what it measures

how often the document’s chunks appear in other chunks’ nearest-neighbour lists, as a z-score
1.0


spread_chunk
how evenly a chunk’s similarity is spread over the topic centres, so a chunk that belongs to no topic scores high
0.8


dup_out
share of chunks with a near-duplicate (similarity at least tau, 0.9) in another document
0.8


off_centre
cosine distance from the mean vector of the whole store
0.5


promiscuity
share of all logged queries that retrieved the document
0.5


low_idf
average IDF of the chunk’s words, negated, so common words score high
0.3


redundancy
share of chunks with a near-duplicate in the same document
0.1


spread_doc
how evenly the document’s chunks spread over topics
0


short
share of chunks under 200 characters
0



spread_doc and short are computed but weighted 0, because on their own they scored below chance in vishalakshi’s measurements. spread_doc in particular marks survey documents that cover many topics, which are not noise.
promiscuity is the only feature that needs data from outside the store: a log of which queries retrieved which documents, passed as seen, a dict from doc id to the set of queries. Without it the feature is 0 for every document and the other eight decide the score.
noise_scores turns the features into one score per document and returns every document, most likely noise first, with its title and each feature value. Each feature is first converted to its rank among the documents and rescaled to about -1.7 to 1.7 by robust_z, so one extreme value cannot dominate. The score is then the weighted average using NOISE_W, or your own weights, or a fitted Ranker. Ranks matter here: with plain z-scores, one outlier document on hub dropped the measured AUC from 0.988 to 0.55.

title: quality
text:
The ranker
The fixed weights work without any labels. If you have marked some documents as noise and some as keepers, Ranker learns weights from those marks instead; vishalakshi measured 0.996 AUC that way, from six marked documents and eighteen keepers.
Ranker is a pairwise learning-to-rank model. You give it rows of features, a group for each row, and a target value. Within each group, every pair of rows where one has the higher target becomes a training example, and the model learns weights that score the higher row above the lower one. It is a logistic regression on the feature differences of those pairs, with an L2 penalty, fitted by Newton’s method (iteratively reweighted least squares, IRLS).
For noise, put every document in one group and use 1 for noise and 0 for keep, then pass the fitted ranker to noise_scores(ranker=...). vishalakshi also fits one on its log of search feedback, with one group per query, to re-rank results. weights() shows what the model learned, and to_dict and from_dict save and restore it as plain JSON-compatible data.

title: topics
text:
Topics from the ANN index
A cluster is a group of chunks whose vectors lie close together, which in practice means chunks about the same subject. Two methods find clusters:

usearch can cluster an HNSW index directly. It needs the index to have enough levels, and on a small store it raises Index too small to cluster!.
When that fails, litesearch falls back to its own method. For each vector it asks the index for the k nearest neighbours (8 by default), then builds groups greedily: it starts from the vector whose close neighbours have the highest total similarity, adds its unassigned neighbours to the group, and repeats with the next unassigned vector. A neighbour counts as close when its cosine similarity is at least the median over all neighbour pairs. Each group holds at most max(k, 4) members, so one large subject comes out as several groups of that size. This method works on a store of any size from 4 vectors up.

Every result reports which method ran, as method='usearch' or method='knn'.
Each cluster is named by c-TF-IDF (class-based term frequency, inverse document frequency). A word scores high for a cluster when many of the cluster’s members use it and few other clusters do. Naming by plain word counts would give every cluster the same few common words. A word that appears in every cluster is never used in a name, and words under three letters and common English words (_STOP) are skipped.
ctfidf_labels does the naming and works on any texts, not only store rows: pass one text per member and the cluster number of each member. topic_nodes clusters a store and writes each cluster into the graph tables as a topic entity, with a mention row linking it to each member chunk.

title: topics
text:
Clusters and peers
These two methods on a store answer questions about the shape of the corpus rather than about a query.
store.clusters() divides the whole store into named groups. Use it to show a reader what a corpus is about, or to browse it by subject. It returns AttrDict(clusters, method, note). Each cluster is AttrDict(centroid, size, label, member_keys, members): member_keys holds the rowids of every member, members holds the rows of the first 24 (set by members=), and the list is sorted largest cluster first.
store.peers(rowid) returns the other members of the cluster that one row belongs to. It returns AttrDict(hits, method, note), with the members in cluster order.
peers and ann_neighbors both start from a row, and they answer different questions. ann_neighbors returns a fixed number of nearest rows (15 by default), however far away the last one is. peers returns the row’s group, which may be smaller and only holds rows that clustered together. When peers cannot use a cluster, because the store has fewer than 4 vectors, the row was left in no cluster, or its cluster has only itself, it returns the limit nearest rows from ann_neighbors instead and sets method='ann'.
Both methods always fill note with a sentence saying what happened, such as 6 clusters over 60 vectors (knn) or index holds 1 vectors; too few to cluster. An empty result looks the same whether the store is too small, has no vectors yet, or has no ANN index, and note tells them apart.
The clustering is computed once and cached on the connection. It is recomputed when the index changes size or when you pass different min_count, max_count or k, so calling peers for many rows in a row is cheap.
The example below builds two clearly separated sets of 30 vectors, one for texts about tensors and one about invoices. The fallback method splits each set into groups of up to 8, and every group is named after the words of its own set.

    min_count:int=None, # usearch: smallest cluster to emit
    max_count:int=None, # usearch: largest cluster to emit
    k:int=8, # neighbours per node in the kNN fallback
    min_size:int=2, # drop groups smaller than this
    label_k:int=4, # words per cluster name
    members:int=24, # member rows fetched per cluster
    columns:list=None, # store columns to return per member row
    max_label_chars:int=4000, # characters of each member's text used for naming
    dtype:type=float16
):
Divide the store into clusters of similar chunks, each named by the words that set it apart.



# clusters(): two well-separated blobs -> two groups, each labelled by its own vocabulary
from litesearch.core import database
_cdb = database()
_cst = _cdb.get_store('cl', ann=True, ndim=8, metric='cosine')
_rs  = np.random.RandomState(0)
_a   = np.concatenate([np.ones((30,4)), np.zeros((30,4))], 1) + _rs.randn(30,8)*0.05
_b   = np.concatenate([np.zeros((30,4)), np.ones((30,4))], 1) + _rs.randn(30,8)*0.05
_txt = [f'kernel gradient tensor sample {i}' for i in range(30)] + [f'invoice ledger payment row {i}' for i in range(30)]
_cst.insert_all([{'content':t,'embedding':v.astype(np.float16).tobytes()}
                 for t,v in zip(_txt, np.concatenate([_a,_b]))])
assert _cst.rebuild_index() == 60
_cl = _cst.clusters(min_size=3)
print(_cl.note, '|', [(c.size, c.label) for c in _cl.clusters][:4])
assert len(_cl.clusters) >= 2, _cl.note
assert _cl.method in ('usearch','knn')
_labels = ' '.join(c.label for c in _cl.clusters)
assert 'tensor' in _labels or 'kernel' in _labels, _labels     # c-TF-IDF names a group after what only it says
assert all(r['rowid'] in c.member_keys for c in _cl.clusters for r in c.members)

# peers(): every member of a group has the rest of that group as its family
_c0 = first(_cl.clusters, lambda c: 'kernel' in c.label or 'tensor' in c.label)
_pr = _cst.peers(_c0.centroid, limit=5, columns=['content'])
print(_pr.note, '|', [h['content'][:24] for h in _pr.hits])
assert _pr.hits and _pr.method == _cl.method, _pr.note
assert all('kernel' in h['content'] for h in _pr.hits), _pr.hits
# a row the clustering left on its own still gets an answer -- with the fallback named in `note`
_solo = first(range(1, 61), lambda r: not _cst.peers(r).method == _cl.method)
if _solo: assert 'nearest neighbours' in _cst.peers(_solo).note

# degradation is reported, never silent
_tiny = database().get_store('tiny', ann=True, ndim=4, metric='cosine')
_tiny.insert_all([{'content':'x','embedding':np.zeros(4,dtype=np.float16).tobytes()}])
_tiny.rebuild_index()
assert _tiny.clusters().clusters == [] and 'too few' in _tiny.clusters().note
assert 'nearest neighbours' in _tiny.peers(1).note
assert database().get_store('plain').clusters().note.endswith('is not an ANN store')
assert database().get_store('empty', ann=True).clusters().note.endswith('has no vectors yet')

Installing litesearch adds a litesearch command. It has one subcommand, install, which copies the SKILL.md file bundled with the package into a project so that coding agents find it. title: configuration tiers
text:
What this measures
litesearch offers many choices: four chunk sizes, five encoders, late chunking, a document tree, an entity graph, clustering, a reranker, and two ways to prepare a keyword query. This notebook reports which combination works best for each of three kinds of document, and groups the results into configuration tiers, from a keyword-only setup with no model up to the most expensive one.
The measurements come from python -m evals.run, in evals/. It builds 45 stores and takes hours, so the harness lives there and this notebook only prints its tables. The full report and the tier definitions are in docs/rag_tiers.md. The cells are eval: false and have no saved output; run them from the repository root after the harness has run.
Several defaults have changed since this was measured, and partly because of it. chunk_markdown now cuts at 512 bytes, db.search now sends its keyword query through pre(), late chunking was deleted (its code is in evals/latechunk.py), and the graph leg was removed from context. Where the sections below describe a default, they describe the one in place at the time.
The three genres were chosen because each breaks retrieval in a different way:








genre
what it is
what makes it hard




regulatory
8 EU directives and regulations, 489 pages
real hierarchy, and the same terms repeated across documents


arxiv
12 papers from cs and astro-ph
headings do not survive PDF conversion, and mathematical notation does not survive at all


astrology
7 books printed between 1822 and 1920, 1,275 pages
archaic prose, CHAPTER XI in the text instead of markup, and one book with no headings



The astro-ph papers are there on purpose. They talk about Mars, conjunctions and ascending nodes, but not in the way the astrology books do, so they test whether a retriever tells the genres apart or only matches words.


Ground truth without an LLM
Each query starts from a sentence that occurs exactly once in the corpus, so the passage and the section it belongs to are known. The sentence is then reworded in five flavours of increasing difficulty: verbatim, degraded, keyword, paraphrase and kw_para. All five are built from the same source sentences, so every comparison here is paired: two configurations are always scored on the same questions.
A result is scored by word 5-grams, runs of five words, that occur in only one section. That works at three levels (passage, section and document), and it does not change when the chunk size does, which matters because chunk size turns out to be the variable with the largest effect. Most tables report section MRR: the mean over queries of 1 divided by the rank of the first result from the right section.

from evals import tables, report as R
from evals.queries import build as build_queries, FLAVOURS, overlap
print(tables._corpus())


qs = build_queries('astrology')
for fl in FLAVOURS: print(f'{fl:<11} {qs[3][fl]}')



1. Chunk size
The four settings are page (one chunk per page) and chunks of at most 1,024, 512 and 256 characters, cut by chonkie’s RecursiveChunker. This was the largest effect in the whole evaluation. When it ran, the default chunker was FastChunker(chunk_size=4096) and add_doc fed it one section at a time, so on pages of 1,700 to 3,500 characters it almost never split anything: the default behaved like page. The default is now 512, counted in UTF-8 bytes: 512 characters of English, about 170 of Devanagari.

print(R.summary('grain', ['genre','chunking','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))



2. Encoder
An encoder turns text into an embedding, a vector of numbers placed so that texts with similar meaning sit close together. The five encoders tested, potion-32M, bge-small, jina-v2-sm, egemma-300m and nomic-v1.5, span three orders of magnitude of cost per chunk. All produce float16 vectors and all ran on the same 4 CPU cores.

print(R.summary('encoder', ['genre','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))



3. Retrieval strategy
A strategy is how the keyword side and the vector side of a search are run and combined. When this was measured, db.search quoted each token of the query, which made its keyword query match only rows holding every token. pre() turns a query into keywords with wildcards joined by OR, and the caller had to know to apply it. db.search now applies it by default (fts_pre=True).

print(R.summary('strategy', ['genre','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))



4. Structure
A flat store, the document tree, and the tree rebuilt with headings recovered from the PDF, since PDF conversion loses most of them.

print(R.summary('structure', ['genre','mode','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))



5. Late chunking
Late chunking embeds a whole document with a long-context encoder and then splits the result into chunk vectors, so each chunk’s vector carries some of its surroundings. It measured worse than embedding chunks on their own and has since been deleted.

print(R.summary('late', ['genre','mode','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))



6. The graph leg
A third ranked list, built by walking a graph of the entities that chunks mention, fused with the keyword and vector lists. It measured negative and is no longer part of context; it lives on in vruksha.

print(R.summary('graph', ['genre','strategy','graph_w'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))
print(R.summary('graph_notopic', ['genre','mode','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='same graph, topic nodes removed'))



7. Clustering
Clustering is judged here as a map of the corpus, by whether its groups follow the genres and sections, not by whether it improves ranking.

print(tables._cluster())



8. One store or three
All three genres in one store against one store per genre. The second table reports how many of the top 10 hits come from the wrong genre.

title: ingestion performance
text:
What this measures
The retrieval evals measure what litesearch finds. This one measures what it costs to put documents in: parsing, chunking, embedding, SQLite writes, keeping the vector index up to date, and building an entity graph. A corpus of a million documents fails on the write side long before it fails on the read side, and the retrieval evals would never have shown that.
Everything here runs through evals/ingest_bench.py, on the same evals.corpus documents the retrieval evals use, split into as many documents as a run needs. hash_embed, a model-free hashing embedder from litesearch.utils, stands in for the encoder, so the timings are litesearch’s own overhead and not model inference. Pass --encoder potion to put a real model back in.
Read the exponent, not the throughput. A cost per document only means something if it stays constant as the corpus grows. Each sweep over corpus sizes reports the slope of log(time) against log(number of documents): 1.0 means time grows in proportion to the corpus, and a slope near 2.0 means doubling the corpus quadruples the time, which never reaches a million documents on any hardware. The most important number in this notebook is that add_dir went from 1.72 to 0.91.
The cells are eval: false because a full sweep takes tens of minutes. The markdown under each cell records its output, measured on 4 CPUs with SQLite in WAL mode, for versions 0.1.15 and 0.1.16.
Three things have changed since. The graph code (build_graph, resolve_entities) moved to vruksha, and the graph benchmarks import it from there. add_dir now parses files on a process pool once at least four of them are slow to parse (PDF, XML, HTML, notebooks), which closes the open item at the end of section 4. 1. Adding documents, at growing corpus sizes

Benchmark on an idle machine. A concurrent nbdev-test run, 2 workers on 4 CPUs, was enough to turn the 50-document case into 55.9s against 3.7s, with every vector count unchanged.


2. Writes: one transaction, and the FTS triggers
process_content called insert_all outside any transaction, so each chunk was committed separately and SQLite’s write-ahead log was flushed to disk each time. Batching in one transaction already existed, but only behind parallel=True, a flag that was meant to be about concurrency. process_content now always writes in transactions of chunk rows. (Since then parallel has become a no-op.)
The remaining gap between a store with full-text search and one without comes from the triggers that update the FTS index on every row. bulk_load removes those triggers for the duration of a load and then rebuilds the FTS index once with FTS5’s rebuild command.

Two separate problems, each costing more than it looked.
ast.get_source_segment splits the entire source file into lines on every call, and pyparse called it once for each chunk it produced, so the cost grew with the number of top-level definitions times the size of the file. Over 400 files of transformers, ast._splitlines_no_ff took 47.3s of 70.0s. pyparse also walked the whole syntax tree to tag each node with its parent and then kept the nodes whose parent was the module, which is exactly the list tree.body already holds.
dir2chunks and pkg2chunks also ran file_parse on a thread pool. Parsing is ast.parse plus a pure-Python walk and holds Python’s global interpreter lock (GIL) throughout, so the threads queued behind each other instead of running together.

5. Graph
The entity graph links chunks through the people, places and terms they mention. Its builder now lives in vruksha, but these fixes were measured here. Profiling found three problems: throughput, memory, and a loss of recall that no timing would have shown.
Throughput. insert_chunk took 9.3s of a 36.1s build. build_graph wrote entities, mentions and edges with insert_all outside any transaction, the same commit-per-batch problem just fixed in process_content. One write_txn around the writes took 1,000 chunks from 21.6s to 11.5s.
Cores. With the writes fixed, extracting entities was 88% of a build (26.6s of 30.3s). Extraction depends only on each chunk’s text, so the build is a parallel map followed by a cheap serial merge. n_workers= runs the map on processes; threads do not help, because yake and spaCy are Python code that holds the GIL. For spaCy the builder uses spaCy’s own n_process, which forks once around the loaded pipeline instead of sending the pipeline to every task. A batch of fewer than MIN_PARALLEL_CHUNKS (200) chunks runs serially.
Both pools keep chunks in order, and the merge relies on that: ents.setdefault keeps the kind recorded at an entity’s first mention, so a different order would relabel entities.
Memory. build_graph held every entity, mention, edge and co-occurrence window for the whole call. A co-occurrence window is a span of text, one per sentence, in which two entities count as appearing together. Windows were the term that never levels off. The number of distinct entities grows ever more slowly (Heaps’ law) and mentions can be written out as they go, but windows keep coming at one per sentence. Peak memory grew in a straight line with the corpus, so the machine’s memory set the limit.
Three changes fixed it, and each was checked to produce a byte-identical graph:

batch= writes mentions out after each batch and moves windows into a scratch SQLite table. _pmi_edges already read its windows twice, because the cut-off for over-connected entities is only known after the first pass, so any object with __len__ and a repeatable __iter__ can stand in for the list.
Pair counting moved into SQL. It was the last structure without a bound: the number of pairs grows with the square of the window size, so the counter kept growing with the corpus even after the windows were no longer held in memory. SQLite groups the pairs in a temporary B-tree on disk instead.
for c in L(chunks) became a plain loop. L() builds a list, so a caller who passed a generator to keep the corpus out of memory had it read into a list before the first chunk was processed.

Recall. Entity resolution merges different spellings of the same entity, and _lexical_pairs proposes candidate pairs from groups of names that share a token. It skipped any group larger than max_group. Groups grow with the corpus, so the skipped pairs were exactly the ones a larger corpus added, and resolution got quietly worse the more text it saw. Large groups are now handled in windows over the sorted names instead of being skipped. Sorting puts variants that contain each other side by side (“polonium” beside “polonium isotope”), which is the case the lexical pass exists for, and the work stays proportional to the group size times max_group.

bench_graph(sizes=(1000,2000), n_workers=4)      # extraction on a process pool
bench_lexical_recall(sizes=(250,500,1000,2000))   # exhaustive O(E^2) ground truth
bench_graph_memory(sizes=(2000,4000,8000))        # run per-size in its own process for a clean RSS

resolve n=1000           7.43s    3.28s
resolve n=2000          13.26s    5.62s
resolve exponent          1.35     1.08

  2000            113 MB               82 MB

The extra memory per chunk halves each time the corpus doubles. It now follows the number of distinct entities, which levels off, rather than the size of the corpus, which does not.
Recall of lexical blocking, against an exhaustive check of every pair with _lex_ok:
entities   truth pairs   skipping (before)   windowing (after)
   1,377         1,569              97.0%              99.8%

   8,487        15,004              75.9%              97.2%
At 8,487 entities the old blocking proposed only three quarters of the valid merges, and the share was falling. Windowing examines 2.2 times as many pairs and costs no measurable time (resolve_entities at n=2000 takes 5.62s against 5.65s), because _toks is cached and _uf_union skips pairs that are already merged. It finds more merges: 6,422 against 5,896.

Determinism
resolve_entities does not give the same answer twice. Rebuilt from scratch at n=2000, it reported merged=5896 on one run and merged=5891 on the next, a difference of about 0.1%.
The batching is not the cause. usearch builds its HNSW graph on several threads, so two builds from the same vectors give slightly different graphs, and an approximate search over a different graph returns slightly different neighbours. This was true before the change as well. The check that tells the two causes apart keeps the index fixed and varies only the probe:

from evals.ingest_bench import verify_ann_probe, verify_resolve
verify_ann_probe(n=2000)          # one fixed index, batched vs the per-entity loop
verify_resolve(sizes=(1000,2000), reps=2)   # full rebuilds: shows the ~0.1% drift

== ann probe equivalence (8487 entities, fixed index, k=8) ==
  looped  x3: 67896 pairs, stable: True
  batched x3: 67896 pairs, stable: True
  identical: True   symmetric difference: 0
On the same index the two probes agree exactly and each is deterministic. The batching is therefore equivalent, and the drift comes from building the index. Expect it if you compare two graph builds.
verify_resolve reports a hash of the partition, which entities ended up grouped together, rather than of the map from each entity to its canonical name. _uf_union breaks ties by arrival order, so which member of a group becomes canonical can change even when the groups do not.



Sharding, considered and set aside
Splitting the data into one database per profile was measured and does not pay for itself.
Before the fixes it made ingestion 4.7x faster at 8 shards, but only because each shard was smaller, which shrank the quadratic cost. The fix alone on one database (19.8s for 400 documents) beat 8 shards without the fix (23.8s). With ingestion linear, sharding adds about 12% and then levels off.
Reads take a few milliseconds either way at this corpus size. Searching 16 shards takes 34.9ms against 8.0ms for one index, and going straight to a known shard saves 6ms. Neither is a reason to restructure anything.
bench_shards and bench_shard_reads stay in evals/ingest_bench.py for the one case where sharding might still help: an HNSW index too large to keep in memory. That is a question of RAM, not speed.


Open at a million documents
These were the open items when this was measured.

Embedding is left out of every number here. With litesearch’s own overhead out of the way, the encoder is now the largest cost, and it is the part that wants a GPU or a process pool.
add_dir parsed files one at a time. It now uses a process pool for slow-to-parse files.
build_graph uses more cores, not more machines. At 207 chunks/s on 4 cores, a million chunks takes about 1.3 hours. The merge is serial, so more cores help until it becomes the bottleneck.
n_workers with a small batch pays the pool’s start-up cost once per batch: 4.87s without batching against 5.33s at batch=500.
build_graph memory grows more slowly than the corpus but still grows. What remains is the entity vocabulary and the edge dict, both of which level off rather than stay flat. The measured slope is fine to a million documents; measure again before ten million.
spaCy extracts about 1.7 times as many entities as the yake fallback but is slower (9.5 against 16.4 chunks/s, measured under tracemalloc). Which is the better trade for retrieval quality has not been measured.

text:
Detecting structure
build_tree needs to know what marks a new section in a document. detect_mode looks for four kinds of signal and picks one mode per document:








mode
sections start at
typical source




markdown
# headings
markdown files, PDFs converted to markdown


verse
verse citations such as || Mn_1.1 ||, and # headings
Sanskrit texts from GRETIL or TEI


chapter
lines like CHAPTER IV, Article 12 or ADHYAYA 3
scanned or plain-text books and legislation


window
every 8 pages
anything with none of the above



The window mode is the fallback, so every document gets a tree of some kind. A document counts as markdown with at least 2 headings if it has up to 3 pages, and otherwise at least 3 headings or one per 25 pages, whichever is more, so a one-page note with a single heading becomes one window. Some PDF converters mark every bold line as a top-level heading. When a document has more than 4 headings per page, all at the same depth, detect_mode does not trust them and uses chapter lines or windows instead.
In chapter mode, struct_levels decides how the structural words nest. Known words have a fixed order: BOOK, TITLE, PART and similar come first, then CHAPTER, then SECTION, then ARTICLE, RULE and CLAUSE. Levels are then renumbered from 1 with no gaps, so a document that only uses “Article” gets its articles at level 1. At most 4 levels are kept.
detect_mode checks for verse mode first. It chooses verse when at least 3 pages carry a citation, citations appear on more than a fifth of the pages, they name at least two levels (such as chapter and verse), and they outnumber markdown headings.

TreeNode
def TreeNode(
    seq:int, title:str, level:int, parent:int | None=None, page_start:int=0, page_end:int=0, segments:list=<factory>,
    children:list=<factory>, summary:str=''
)->None:
One section of a document, where seq is its position in the node list and parent is the seq of the section above it.


build_tree takes a list of (page number, text) pairs and returns the nodes as a flat list, where nodes[seq] is the node with that seq and each node’s parent is its parent’s seq. The same list is written to the nodes table, and toc() rebuilds the nesting when you ask for it. A heading is placed under the nearest earlier heading of a shallower level, so a document that starts at ## or jumps from # to ### still nests correctly.
In verse mode, a citation like Mn_1.1 gives the verse’s address: every part except the last names the division it belongs to, so Mn_1.1 opens a node Mn 1 for chapter 1. Verse mode also reads # headings, because some texts name their sections (## dhyanam) and carry no citations. Citation levels are counted from the heading above them.
heading_path builds the breadcrumb for a node. If a segment repeats the one before it, it is dropped, so a PDF whose first heading is the same as the document title reads Field Manual › Chapter 1 and not Field Manual › Field Manual › Chapter 1.
The breadcrumb is stored with every chunk in the heading column, and by default it is also prepended to the chunk’s text before embedding, so the vector reflects where the text sits. It is not added to the full-text index: a keyword search for a section title finds only chunks whose own text contains it.

```python

```

text:
The tables
get_tree adds three tables beside a chunk store and four columns to the store. The chunk store is still an ordinary store, so full-text search, the ANN index and db.search work on it unchanged.
docs    id · title · source · kind · pages · meta · hash · added_at
sources source · doc_id · added_at
nodes   id ('doc#seq') · doc_id · parent_id · level · seq · title ·
        page_start · page_end · summary · nchunks
store   content · embedding · metadata · doc_id · node_id · page · heading   [+ FTS5, +ANN]
For the default store the tables are called docs and nodes; for a store called papers they are papers_docs, papers_sources and papers_nodes.
A document’s id is a hash of its source and its title. A file’s source is its resolved path, so a relative path, an absolute path and a symlink to one file are one source. hash is a hash of the document’s (page, text) pairs, and sources maps every source to the document holding its text:

The same source with the same text again is skipped as unchanged.
The same source with changed text replaces the old chunks and nodes, and keeps the id.
A different source with text already stored is skipped as same text as <source>, and gains a row in sources pointing at the stored document. A copy, or a string with the same text, adds no chunks.
A document goes when the last source pointing at it does. delete_source forgets one source. delete_doc forgets the document’s own source; text another source shares stays, under that source. Editing a file whose text another source shares moves the old text to an id of its own for that source first.
A text added with no source is keyed by its title. A second, different text under the same title is skipped, as before 0.1.50, because a title names nothing on disk.

text:
Ingestion
There are three ways in, from the most control to the least:

add_doc takes text you have already extracted, as a string or a list of (page number, text) pairs. It builds the tree, chunks each section, embeds the chunks with emb_fn and stores them. Use it when your app fetches or converts documents itself.
add_file reads one file and passes its pages to add_doc.
add_dir does the same for every document file under a folder, or for a list of files.

Each returns a dict per document with its doc_id, title, kind, number of nodes and number of chunks, or a skipped reason when its text is already stored: unchanged, or same text as <source>.
emb_fn takes a list of strings and returns one vector per string. Without it, chunks are stored with no embedding, which is enough for keyword search, toc and read.
Chunks are cut within each section, never across a section boundary, using chunk_markdown’s default chunker unless you pass chunker=, any chonkie chunker. A chunk shorter than 40 characters is joined to the chunk before it instead of being stored alone. Two chunks with the same text in different sections are both kept, because the row id is a hash of the node id and the text.
A chunker sees one segment of a section at a time. Some readers produce very small segments, such as one verse per page, and a chunker aiming at 700 characters never reaches that size on a 60-character verse. A chunker can ask for its small chunks to be joined across segments by having pack_cited=True and a target size; pack_target reads the size a chunker asks for, and _pack_segments then joins consecutive chunks of one node up to target characters. Ordinary chunkers have neither attribute and are unaffected.
add_doc(defer=...) collects the chunks in a list instead of embedding and storing them, and store_chunks embeds and stores such a list later. add_doc(jobs=...) collects the whole write, and _commit stores a batch of them: chunks first, then nodes, doc rows and sources. add_dir uses this to embed chunks from many documents in batches of 2,000 (embed_batch), which is faster than one call per document, and a run that fails before a batch is stored leaves the documents it would have replaced whole.

add_dir ingests every file under dir whose extension is in types, or exactly the paths in files=. Files whose text is already stored are skipped, and a file edited since it was added is replaced. Each call writes to one store, because the embedder and the ANN index belong to that store; to send files from one folder to different stores, call it once per store with files=.
Parsing PDFs, notebooks and XML is slow, so when 4 or more such files are in the batch, add_dir parses them in a pool of worker processes (n_workers overrides this; 0 means no pool). In one measurement, parsing took 3.55 of the 5.31 seconds needed to ingest 8 PDFs, while 150 markdown files took 2.7 milliseconds to read in total, too little for a pool to help, and HTML is read the same way. All writes stay in the main process.
By default the full-text index is updated as each chunk is written. With bulk=True, add_dir turns that off during the load and rebuilds the full-text index once at the end. This is faster for a large first load, but keyword search misses the new documents until the load finishes, so use it only when nothing searches the store meanwhile. The ANN index is rebuilt once at the end either way.

These functions read the tree and compute no embeddings, so they are fast and need no encoder. They suit an agent or a reader that browses: look at the table of contents, pick “the chapter on remedies”, and open it.

text:
Retrieval that knows about structure
Hybrid search runs two searches and combines them. The keyword search uses SQLite FTS5, a full-text index ranked by bm25, which favours chunks that contain the query’s rarer words. The vector search compares the query’s embedding with each chunk’s embedding. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges the two ranked lists: each chunk scores 1/(rrf_k + rank) in each list it appears in, so a chunk ranked well by both searches beats one ranked well by only one. rrf_k defaults to 60.
doc_search is db.search for a tree store, with two additions. Every hit gets a breadcrumb. And hits from the same section at most gap pages apart (1 by default) are joined into one hit, so a reader gets one passage instead of two halves; the joined hit keeps the best rank and score of its parts and counts them in _nspan. rerank=True reorders the top 30 candidates with a flashrank cross-encoder, a small model that reads the query and each chunk together; it is slower and downloads a 3 MB model on first use.
sections answers “which sections match”, returning sections instead of chunks. It gathers chunk hits (limit × fanout, at least 20), groups them by node, and scores each section by its best hit (score='max'). Each section comes with its breadcrumb, summary, page range, up to per snippets and a read string naming the call that opens it. score='mean' averages the hits and score='sum' adds them. Summing favours long sections that collect many weak hits: on 150 known-item queries over 486 pages of EU legislation (07_doc_eval), sections scored 0.852 MRR with sum against 0.957 with max on verbatim queries, and 0.304 against 0.505 on reworded ones.
Use doc_search when you want passages to show or quote. Use sections when the answer is a place in a document, such as which article or chapter, and you will read it next.
doc_search(adaptive=True) changes the weight of each list before fusion using adaptive_weights, three fixed rules: when one search returns nothing, the other gets all the weight; a quoted phrase adds 0.6 to the keyword weight; and a query where at least half the words look like names or identifiers (capitalised, containing digits or underscores) adds 0.4. It is off by default because on the natural-language queries in 07_doc_eval the rules never fired.

title: doc eval
text:
litesearch.tree splits each document into a tree of sections (title, chapter, section, article) and records, for every chunk, the section it came from. The argument for building it was that a chunk which knows where it lives should retrieve better. This notebook tests that argument against the litesearch that came before the tree.
The corpus is the one recorded in the outputs below: 11 PDFs and 524 pages, almost all of it EU directives and regulations, plus the Attention paper. Legislation was chosen because it has real hierarchy (TITLE, CHAPTER, SECTION, Article), which is the kind of document the tree was built for.
Four systems share one corpus, one encoder and one query set:



system
what it is




flat-page
litesearch before the tree: chunk_markdown on each page, searched with db.search


flat-fine
the tree’s own chunk texts in a plain store, with no sections and no headings


tree
db.add_doc and db.doc_search: chunks linked to sections, embedded with their heading, adjacent hits merged into spans


sections
db.sections: the same search rolled up so that each result is a whole section



flat-fine is the control that matters. The tree also chunks more finely than one chunk per page, and without this control it would take credit for an effect that any store gets by using smaller chunks.
The encoder is a weak stand-in. The machine this ran on could not reach huggingface.co, so no ONNX or model2vec model could be downloaded. The vector side of each search uses LSA instead: TF-IDF word weights reduced to 256 dimensions with a truncated SVD, fitted on this corpus. Every system uses it, so the comparisons between systems hold, but absolute scores understate anything that depends on the meaning of the text, heading context most of all.

class LSA:
    "TF-IDF + truncated SVD, fitted on the corpus. Stands in for an ONNX model — see the caveat above."
    def __init__(self, dim=256):
        from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
        from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
        from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
        from sklearn.preprocessing import Normalizer
        self.p = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2, max_df=0.5,
                                               stop_words='english', ngram_range=(1,2)),
                               TruncatedSVD(n_components=dim, random_state=0), Normalizer(copy=False))
    def fit(self, t): self.p.fit(list(t)); return self
    def __call__(self, t, **kw): return self.p.transform(list(t)).astype(np.float16)

text:
Queries and ground truth
Each query is one sentence of 9 to 26 words copied from an Article, at most one per Article and 150 in all. Each sentence is asked in two forms:

verbatim, the sentence as printed. FTS5 answers this almost trivially, so it only checks that nothing got worse.
degraded, with the rarest 45% of its words removed. This is not a paraphrase, but it removes the exact-match shortcut and leaves something like what a person types when they do not know the wording.

A result counts as a hit when the text a system returns contains the original sentence. That test does not depend on how the system chunked the document.

_ART, _SENT = re.compile(r'^\s*#*\s*Article\s+\d+', re.I), re.compile(r'[^.!?\n]{60,240}[.!?]')
arts = {i: n for i, n in nodes.items() if _ART.match(n['title'] or '')}
def owner(nid):
    seen = set()
    while nid and nid not in seen:
        seen.add(nid)
        if nid in arts: return nid
        nid = (nodes.get(nid) or {}).get('parent_id')
by_node = {}
for r in trows: by_node.setdefault(r['node_id'], []).append(r['content'])

rnd = random.Random(0); aids = list(arts); rnd.shuffle(aids)
qs = []
for a in aids:
    for m in _SENT.finditer(' '.join(by_node.get(a, []))):
        s = ' '.join(m.group(0).split()).strip('. ')
        if 9 <= len(s.split()) <= 26 and not s.startswith(('http','- [','|')): qs.append((s, a)); break
    if len(qs) >= 150: break

df = Counter(w.lower().strip('.,;:()') for t in all_text for w in t.split())
def degrade(q, keep=0.55):
    ws = q.split()
    if len(ws) < 6: return q
    rare = sorted(range(len(ws)), key=lambda i: df.get(ws[i].lower().strip('.,;:()'), 0))
    drop = set(rare[:max(1, int(len(ws)*(1-keep)))])
    return ' '.join(w for i, w in enumerate(ws) if i not in drop)
dqs = [(degrade(q), a, q) for q, a in qs]
print(f'{len(qs)} queries, {len(arts)} Article nodes indexed')
print(f'  verbatim : {qs[0][0][:86]}')
print(f'  degraded : {dqs[0][0][:86]}')

def nrm(s): return ' '.join((s or '').lower().split())
def score_text(runs, k=10):
    r1=r5=rk=0; mrr=0.0
    for q, ts in runs:
        r = next((i for i,t in enumerate(ts[:k]) if nrm(q) in nrm(t)), None)
        if r is None: continue
        rk += 1; mrr += 1/(r+1); r1 += r==0; r5 += r<5
    n = max(1,len(runs)); return dict(r1=r1/n, r5=r5/n, r10=rk/n, mrr=mrr/n)
def score_art(runs, k=5):
    r1=r3=rk=0; mrr=0.0
    for gt, got in runs:
        r = next((i for i,a in enumerate(got[:k]) if a==gt), None)
        if r is None: continue
        rk += 1; mrr += 1/(r+1); r1 += r==0; r3 += r<3
    n = max(1,len(runs)); return dict(r1=r1/n, r3=r3/n, r5=rk/n, mrr=mrr/n)
def show(nm, s): print(f'  {nm:<24} ' + '  '.join(f'{k}={v:.3f}' for k,v in s.items()))

plain = lambda db, tbl, q, k=10: [h['content'] for h in (db.search(q, E(q), columns=['content'],
                        limit=k, table_name=tbl, dtype=np.float16) or [])]
tree_hits = lambda db, q, k=10, **kw: [h['content'] for h in db.doc_search(q, E(q), limit=k, dtype=np.float16, **kw)]
SYS = {'flat-page (before)':   lambda q: plain(fdb,'flat',q),

C. Which Article answers this
This is the question a reader asks of a legal corpus. Each system’s results are mapped to Articles in the same way, so the mapping is not a variable: an exact chunk match first, then any Article whose text overlaps the returned passage. c2a, a2text = {}, {}
for r in trows:

a2text = {a: nrm(' '.join(v)) for a, v in a2text.items()}
a_keys = [(a, t[:200]) for a, t in a2text.items() if len(t) > 60]

def to_arts(texts, k=5):

        if a and a not in out: out.append(a)

for label, qset in (('verbatim', [(q,a) for q,a in qs]), ('degraded', [(d,a) for d,a,_ in dqs])):

sections() can score a section by the best of its hits (score='max'), their mean, or their sum. Summing favours long sections: a long chapter with five weak hits outranks the short Article that answers the question. flat-page shows what page-sized chunks cannot do. On verbatim queries it puts the right text first 94% of the time, but it names the right Article first only 27% of the time, because one page spans several Articles and the chunk cannot say which. That is the case for the tree that these numbers support.

title: postfix
text:
Making usearch safe to load: fetch its SQLite extension once, check it in a throwaway process, and fall back to numpy when it fails.

litesearch uses two compiled parts of the usearch package. Its HNSW index is a Python extension. Its vector distance functions for SQL are a SQLite extension that usearch downloads from GitHub the first time usearch.sqlite_path() is called.
usearch_fix adds /usr/lib to the SQLite extension’s rpath with Apple’s install_name_tool, without which the extension cannot find the system SQLite on macOS. It does nothing on Linux and Windows, prints failures instead of raising them, and prints each step with v=True. litesearch calls it before the first load, so you do not call it yourself.

title: postfix
section: Probing usearch before the first load
text:
Probing usearch before the first load
Loading usearch’s SQLite extension has crashed Python with a segmentation fault on GitHub’s AMD EPYC 9V74 and 9V45 runners, about one run in four, at loadextension in database(). A crash in a compiled library cannot be caught, so litesearch tests usearch in a throwaway subprocess before it loads anything into your process.
The probe builds a 4-number HNSW index and searches it, then loads the SQLite extension into an in-memory database and calls distance_cosine_f32. It runs once per machine. Its verdict is cached in cache_dir()/usearch.json, keyed by the CPU model, the usearch version and the extension’s size in bytes, so a new usearch release or a new download probes again. A part that fails is turned off, with one warning per process:

SQLite extension off: vec_search computes distances with numpy.
HNSW index off: get_index returns an ExactIndex, which searches every vector with numpy, so ann_search, ann_neighbors, sync, rebuild_index, Database.search(ann=True) and Index.search return exact results.

usearch writes its download straight to its final path, so a second process can load a half-written file. usearch_lib downloads under a file lock in cache_dir(). When the HNSW index passes and the extension fails, the extension is downloaded once more and probed again, since a half-written file fails the same way. A failed download is not cached.
To override the probe, set LITESEARCH_USEARCH:

LITESEARCH_USEARCH=0 keeps usearch out of the process, with no probe and no warning.
LITESEARCH_USEARCH=1 uses usearch with no probe.

To probe again, delete usearch.json. LITESEARCH_CACHE moves the cache folder.
A usearch that does not import turns both parts off without a probe, since the probe would import it too. On macOS 14, import usearch raises ImportError: symbol not found in flat namespace '_nk_capabilities': every numkong wheel from 7.5 links ___sme_memset, which only macOS 15 has, and usearch 2.26 needs numkong 7.5 or later. litesearch then searches with numpy, with one warning per process. That verdict is not cached, because the import is what decides it.
A frozen app is not probed, because its sys.executable may not run python -c. It imports usearch’s HNSW index in its own process instead, and turns both parts off when that import fails.

title: store
text:
Some search structures are expensive to build and cheap to read: a matrix of every embedding in a store, or a lookup table of folded spellings. A web app usually runs several worker processes, and if each one builds the structure itself, it pays the build time at every start and holds its own copy in memory.
stored builds the arrays once, saves them as .npy files under root/<name>-<key>/, and returns them memory-mapped. A memory-mapped array is read from the file by the operating system as pages are touched, instead of being loaded into the process. Every process that maps the same file shares those pages, so ten workers reading a 100 MB matrix use about 100 MB between them, not 1 GB.
key says what the arrays were built from. Choose something that changes whenever the source data changes: an index’s FTS signature, a row count with the highest rowid, plus the versions of the libraries that shaped the build. When the key changes, stored builds a new set and removes the old sets of the same name. A process that still has an old set mapped keeps reading it safely, since a deleted file stays readable while it is mapped.
The first process to need a set takes a file lock, builds the arrays into a temporary folder and renames the folder into place. Other processes starting at the same moment wait on the lock and then map the finished set, so they never see half-written files and the build runs once. If root cannot be written, stored builds the arrays in memory and returns them unshared. Call it without build in a process that should only read: it returns the set if one exists for that key, and None if not.


source


def stored(
    root, # folder that holds every stored set
    name, # what the arrays are; the prefix of their folder
    key, # what the arrays are built from; a new key triggers a rebuild
    build:NoneType=None, # `() -> {name: array}`; None only maps an existing set, or returns None
)->dict:
Return build()’s arrays memory-mapped from root/<name>-<key>, building them once across all processes.



_root = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
_n = [0]
def _b(): _n[0] += 1; return dict(a=np.arange(5), b=np.array(['x', 'y']))
_s = stored(_root, 'demo', 'k1', _b)
test_eq(_s['a'].tolist(), [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]); assert isinstance(_s['a'], np.memmap)
stored(_root, 'demo', 'k1', _b); test_eq(_n[0], 1)            # built once
stored(_root, 'demo', 'k2', _b); test_eq(_n[0], 2)
test_eq(sorted(p.name for p in _root.glob('demo-*')), ['demo-k2'])   # the older set is gone
test_eq(stored(_root, 'demo', 'k1'), None)                   # no build: only what is there
test_eq(stored(_root, 'demo', 'k2')['a'].tolist(), [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]); test_eq(_n[0], 2)


_pr = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
_src = f"""import numpy as np, time; from pathlib import Path; from litesearch.store import stored
def b(): open(Path({str(_pr)!r})/'built', 'a').write('x'); time.sleep(.3); return dict(a=np.ones(3))
stored({str(_pr)!r}, 'par', 'k', b)"""
_ps = [subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', _src]) for _ in range(3)]
test_eq([p.wait() for p in _ps], [0, 0, 0])
test_eq((_pr/'built').read_text(), 'x')                      # three processes, one build

title: store
text:
A key index
FTS5 matches the tokens its tokenizer produced. Sometimes an app needs to find rows by a key the tokenizer never made: an alias for a name, a romanised title, or a spelling folded by a rule of your own. KeyIndex is an inverted index for that case. For each key it keeps a posting list, the list of row numbers that hold the key, so a lookup returns rows directly without scanning text.
KeyIndex.build(pairs) takes (key, row) pairs and returns plain arrays, which you can pass to stored so every process shares them. KeyIndex(arrays) wraps the arrays for reading. The keys are sorted and packed into one UTF-8 byte string, so lookup(key) is a binary search. It returns the rows holding key, or with prefix=True the rows of every key that starts with key, sorted and without repeats.
Use FTS5 for words in running text. Use KeyIndex when you already know the exact keys each row should answer to.

title: store
text:
A vector matrix
There are two ways to find the stored vectors nearest a query vector. Exact search compares the query with every vector and returns the true nearest. Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) search walks a prebuilt graph, here usearch’s HNSW index from get_store(ann=True), and returns nearly the nearest in far fewer comparisons. ANN is the right choice for a very large store; it costs an index that has to be built and kept in step with the table.
VecMatrix is exact search done fast. It holds a store’s embeddings as one float32 matrix with every row scaled to unit length, so one matrix product with the normalised query gives the cosine similarity of every row at once. There is no index to keep in step. vec_search in litesearch.core is also exact, but it computes each distance in SQL on every query; VecMatrix reads the vectors once and keeps them in memory, or memory-mapped through stored. The matrix takes 4 bytes per dimension per row, so 100,000 rows of 256 dimensions is about 100 MB.
VecMatrix.build(tbl) reads the vectors in rowid order, optionally narrowed by a SQL where, and returns the arrays. Pass the dtype the vectors were stored as; the default is float16. search(q, k) returns (rowid, similarity) pairs, most similar first, with equal scores in row order. rows= limits the search to some positions in the matrix, such as the rows of one book. These are positions, not rowids.
Embeddings have no FTS signature, so pick the stored key yourself: the row count and the highest rowid, or a counter your own writes increase.


source

VecMatrix
def VecMatrix(
    a
):
Search a store’s embeddings by exact cosine similarity, held as one unit-length float32 matrix.



_vd = database(sem_search=False)
_vd.execute('create table v(name text, embedding blob)')
for nm, e in [('a', [1, 0, 0]), ('b', [0, 1, 0]), ('c', [1, 1, 0]), ('none', None)]:
    _vd.execute('insert into v values(?, ?)', [nm, None if e is None else np.array(e, np.float16).tobytes()])
_vm = VecMatrix(VecMatrix.build(_vd.t.v))
test_eq(len(_vm), 3)
_hits = _vm.search(np.array([1, .1, 0], np.float16).tobytes(), k=2)
test_eq([i for i, _ in _hits], [1, 3]); assert _hits[0][1] > _hits[1][1]
test_eq(VecMatrix(VecMatrix.build(_vd.t.v, where="name='b'")).search([0, 1, 0], k=5)[0][0], 2)
_vs = VecMatrix(stored(_root, 'vecs', 'k', lambda: VecMatrix.build(_vd.t.v)))
assert isinstance(_vs.m, np.memmap) and _vs.search([0, 1, 0], k=1)[0][0] == 2
test_eq(VecMatrix(VecMatrix.build(_vd.t.v, where='0')).search([1, 0, 0]), [])
test_eq([i for i, _ in _vm.search([1, 0, 0], k=5, rows=[1, 2])], [3, 2])   # within matrix rows 1 and 2: c, then b
test_eq(_vm.search([1, 0, 0], rows=[]), [])

text:
Before a document can be searched it has to be cut into pieces. A search returns pieces, not whole files: a 15-page paper should come back as the paragraph that answers the question, not as page 1. Each piece is called a chunk, and the object that decides where to cut is a chunker.
This page holds the tools that read files and produce chunks, plus the functions that clean up a query before it reaches SQLite’s full-text search. Most applications never call them directly, because Index.add and add_dir in litesearch.tree call them for you. Reach for them when you build your own pipeline on database(), or when you want to see what a file turns into before you index it.
The sections, in order: reading PDFs, chunking text, reading code and other files, profiles for special document kinds, listing installed packages, preparing queries, and building a PDF from images.

pdf_parse is the function to use when you index a PDF. It returns a list with one markdown string per page. The work is done by pdflite, a separate package whose helpers are re-exported here. pdflite converts each page with pdf_oxide, joins words hyphenated across a line break, and collapses the extra spaces and blank lines the conversion leaves. Some pages come out with their columns scrambled, so that a figure such as a price ends up on a line of its own, away from its label. For those pages pdflite tries the plain-text layer instead and keeps whichever version strands fewer values.
A scanned book has no text layer at all, only page images, and needs OCR (optical character recognition, reading the text from the images). ocr_selection controls it. With 'auto', the default, OCR runs over the whole document when pdf_oxide reports any page as scanned. 'on' always runs it and 'off' never does. OCR needs the liteparse package, which is not installed with litesearch.
Images on the pages are saved to out_path/image_dir, and the markdown links to them by that relative path. With no out_path, they go to pdfs/images under the current folder. preserve_layout=True keeps indentation and runs of spaces, which tables laid out with spaces need.

title: data
text:
Chunking text
The default chunker is chonkie’s FastChunker, set to 512 bytes. It walks through the text and cuts each piece at the last newline, full stop or question mark before the 512-byte limit, so a chunk usually ends at the end of a line or sentence. Where there is none, it cuts at the limit. 512 bytes is about 500 characters of English, or about 170 characters of Devanagari, which takes three bytes per letter. evals/ measured 512-byte chunks against page-sized ones, and the smaller chunks found the right section more often.

SafeFastChunker
FastChunker cuts by byte position, so a cut can land in the middle of a character that takes more than one byte, such as an em dash, a curly quote or any Devanagari letter. It then raises UnicodeDecodeError, and a long unbroken paragraph with one such character, which most scraped web pages contain, is enough to trigger it. SafeFastChunker moves each cut back to the start of the character it split. No text is lost; a cut moves by at most three bytes. litesearch uses it everywhere in place of FastChunker.

There are three ways to chunk text:

chunk_markdown(text) returns the chunks as a list of strings. Use it when you only need the text.
chunk_spans(text) returns (start, end, text) for each chunk, as character positions in the string you passed in. Use it when you need to map a chunk back to its place in the source, for example to highlight a hit inside the full document.
PdfDocument.pdf_chunks() runs pdf_parse and then chunk_markdown on each page, and returns (page, chunk_idx, text). Pages are counted from 1 and chunk_idx restarts at 0 on each page. Use it to index a PDF page by page without building a document tree.

text:
Profiles: how to read one kind of document
Some documents need more than a different chunker. A Sanskrit text in TEI XML, for example, needs a reader that knows an <lg xml:id=...> element is a verse, a tree that treats a citation as the start of a chapter, and a chunker that cuts at the daṇḍa (।), the mark that ends a half-verse. A Profile bundles all of these for one kind of document and gives them a name. When add_file or add_dir in litesearch.tree reads a file, it asks profile_for whether a registered profile claims it. If one does, the profile’s parts are used; if none does, the file goes through the default pipeline above.

Profile
The fields, all optional except name:



field
what it is




exts
the extensions the profile claims, comma-separated, such as '.xml,.txt'; empty claims every extension


detect
a function from the file’s text to True or False, used when an extension is shared


parse
a function from a path to (pages, meta), used instead of the default reader


chunker
a function returning a chonkie chunker, used instead of the 512-byte default


mode
the structure mode for build_tree, used instead of detecting one


kind
the document kind recorded on the document’s row, so searches can filter on it


meta
a function from a chunk’s text to a dict, stored in the chunk’s metadata column



meta lets a profile attach facts that only it can work out. ganapati’s Sanskrit profile stores each verse’s metre there. The metadata column is part of the full-text index that get_store builds, so those facts become searchable and filterable with no change to the table.


profile_for
profile_for returns the first registered profile that claims a file, or None. It checks the extension first and then calls detect on up to the first 60,000 characters of the file. An extension alone is never enough to decide: .xml may be TEI, a vedicreader export or something unrelated, and .txt may be anything. A profile that has no detect and shares its extension with another can still be chosen by passing name=. register_profile adds a profile, replacing any with the same name.

section: Preparing a query for full-text search
text:
Preparing a query for full-text search
SQLite’s full-text search engine, FTS5, finds rows that contain the words of a query and ranks them with bm25, a score that rewards rare words and words that appear often in a short row. Its query language gives several characters a special meaning: * marks a prefix, " quotes a phrase, parentheses group terms, ^ anchors a term to the start of a column, - belongs to the syntax for choosing columns, and OR, AND and NOT combine terms. A word may contain only letters, digits and _ unless it is quoted. A question typed by a user can therefore fail with a syntax error, and even a valid one asks for too much: by default FTS5 returns only rows that contain every word, including words such as “how” and “does”.
These functions turn a user’s text into a query FTS5 accepts and that finds more:

clean replaces the operator characters * , " ( ) ^, and a - directly before a word, with spaces. It returns None for an empty query. Underscores are kept, so fts_search stays one word.
kw splits the text into words with the Unicode word-boundary rules (UAX #29, through apsw), lowercases them, and drops one-letter words and the stopwords in QSTOP, a list of common English words such as “the”, “how” and “does”. If every word is a stopword, it keeps them all.
add_wc adds * to each word so it also matches longer words that start with it: sample* matches “samples”. A word with characters other than ASCII letters, digits and _, such as pathfinder's or any Devanagari word, is quoted first, because FTS5 accepts it only as a quoted string.
mk_wider joins the words with OR, so a row needs only one of them to match. bm25 still ranks rows that match more of the words higher.
pre runs all four in that order: clean, kw, add_wc, mk_wider. Each step after clean can be turned off.

Database.search passes the keyword half of every search through pre unless you set fts_pre=False. evals/ measured it at +0.016 to +0.093 weighted MRR. To build a query from a list of terms you already have, rather than from a user’s sentence, use fts_or, fts_and or fts_phrases in litesearch.core, which quote each term.

text:
Full-text search matches words exactly as they were indexed. SQLite’s FTS5, the full-text engine litesearch uses, splits text into tokens with a tokenizer and stores every token in an index; a query matches a row only when the query’s tokens are in that index. Sanskrit breaks this in three ways. The same word can be printed in Devanagari or in IAST, the Latin transliteration with diacritics. Vedic texts add tone marks above and below the letters. And many readers type a plain-English spelling with no diacritics at all. Before this module, these searches found nothing:

hits

The fix is to reduce every word, whatever its script, to a lossy ASCII key when it is indexed, and to do the same to the query. श्रीमाता, śrīmātā and srimata all become srimata, so each of them finds the other two. Nothing is transliterated at query time and no second column is added.
Every store litesearch creates uses this, Sanskrit or not. English text keeps its own tokens, so an English search behaves as before, but the extra keys do take space: on this repository’s notebooks the FTS index grows 14.7%. text:
Folding a word
Folding means mapping several spellings of a word to one key. This module folds at two strengths.
fold_token is the strict fold. It removes Vedic tone marks (strip_vedic), turns Devanagari into ASCII letter by letter (deva2ascii), and strips diacritics from Latin letters. Aspirates survive: भीष्म folds to bhisma and kṛṣṇa to krsna, and the consonants ś, ṣ and s all become s. detect_script reports whether a string is mostly Devanagari or Latin.
roman_fold is the loose fold, built on fold_token for readers who type English spellings. It drops the h after a consonant (so bh, ch, dh, kh, sh, th all lose it), shortens ee to i, oo to u and any doubled vowel to one, turns w into v, and reads ri before a consonant as the vowel ṛ. Bheeshma, Bhishma, Bhīṣma and भीष्म all become bisma; Krishna and कृष्ण become krsna; chandra and चन्द्र become candra. The ri rule also catches words that never had a ṛ, so śrīmātā folds to srmata. That is harmless in an index, because the query folds the same way.
skeleton goes further still and keeps a folded word’s first letter and its consonants, with vowels and y removed and repeated letters collapsed: saundarya and soundarya both become sndr. It is too loose for an index. correct(skeleton=True) uses it as a last resort when looking for the index term a misspelled query word was meant to be.

text:
The tokenizer
An FTS5 tokenizer is the function that turns a row’s text into the tokens the index stores, and a query’s text into the tokens it looks up. FTS5 lets tokenizers wrap each other: in a chain such as porter unicode61, unicode61 splits the text into words and porter stems each word it receives, so running is stored as run.
sanskrit_tokenizer is a wrapping tokenizer of that kind. It asks the tokenizer inside it for words and passes each word on together with its fold_token key and, for longer words, its roman_fold key. FTS5 calls tokens that share a position colocated: they count as the same word, so a query matches the row through any of them. The original word is kept, so nothing an English search relied on is lost. Passing original=0 drops it and keeps only the keys.
SANSKRIT_TOKENIZE is the tokenizer’s registered name, 'sanskrit'. litesearch’s default chain, _FTS_TOKENIZE in litesearch.core, is porter simplify casefold 1 sanskrit unicodewords. Read it from the right: apsw’s unicodewords splits words by the Unicode rules and keeps fts_search whole, sanskrit adds the folded keys, simplify casefold 1 lowercases every token without removing diacritics, and porter stems English. sanskrit has to sit inside porter. If it wrapped porter instead, it would fold porter’s output, the index would hold dharmaksetre while the query dharmaksetre stems to dharmaksetr, and the search would miss. The regression test below checks exactly this case.
A store’s tokenizer is fixed when its FTS table is created. database() registers sanskrit on every connection it opens, and register_sanskrit does the same for a connection you opened yourself. A connection without it, such as Python’s sqlite3 module or the sqlite3 shell, can still read the store’s ordinary columns, but every FTS query and every insert into the store fails with error in tokenizer constructor, because the insert triggers update the FTS index.

text:
Keyword search finds rows that share words with the query. Semantic search finds rows that mean something close to it, even with no word in common: “car” can find a passage about automobiles. It works by turning each piece of text into an embedding, a fixed-length list of numbers (a vector) placed so that texts with similar meanings sit close together. The model that does this is the encoder. At indexing time the encoder embeds every chunk and the vectors are stored; at query time it embeds the query, and the search returns the chunks whose vectors are nearest.
A query and the documents it searches must be embedded by the same encoder. Vectors from two different models live in unrelated spaces, so comparing them gives meaningless distances without any error. This is why a store records which encoder wrote it (see encoder_id below).
litesearch’s default encoder is static_embedder(), which loads model2vec’s potion-multilingual-128M. A model2vec model is static: it holds one precomputed vector per token and embeds a text by averaging the vectors of its tokens. There is no neural network to run, so it needs no GPU and no ONNX runtime, and it embedded about 8,600 chunks of 500 characters a second on an Apple-silicon Mac. It returns 256-dimensional float32 vectors and covers many scripts, Devanagari included. Index uses it unless you pass another encoder. static_code_embedder() loads potion-code-16M-v2, a model2vec model trained on source code; nothing in litesearch uses it by default, so pass it yourself if you index code. Both functions cache the model per name, so every caller shares one copy. The multilingual model is about 500 MB.
evals/ found that the choice of encoder moves retrieval quality less than chunk size or reranking do. Across four encoders the spread was 0.018 to 0.046 weighted MRR, and the static model won one of the three test corpora outright.
When a transformer is worth the extra time, FastEncode runs one through ONNX Runtime. The dicts in the next cell name models that have been tried with it; each gives the Hugging Face repository, the ONNX file inside it and, where the model needs them, prompt templates. FastEncode runs a text embedding model exported to ONNX, a portable format for neural networks, with ONNX Runtime. It works with most ONNX models that ship a Hugging Face tokenizer. On first use it downloads the model with download_model, which reuses the local Hugging Face cache when the files are already there. FastEncode needs onnxruntime, which is not installed with litesearch (pip install onnxruntime). text:
Image encoding
FastEncodeImage embeds images the way FastEncode embeds text, so you can find pictures that look alike: store a vector per image, embed a query image, and search. It takes Pillow images, file paths or image bytes. Each image is converted to RGB, resized to a square of the model’s input size (224 pixels by default) without cropping, normalised with the model’s mean and standard deviation, and run through the ONNX model. Where the model returns one output per image patch, those are averaged into one vector. The default model is nomic-embed-vision v1.5, with 768-dimensional float16 vectors. batch_size, parallel and stream work as in FastEncode, and the method is embed rather than encode. Like FastEncode, it needs onnxruntime and returns None from embed when the model failed to load.

text:
Text and images in one space
To search images with a text query, the text and image vectors have to come from models trained together, so that a caption and its picture land close to each other. There are two ways to get that here.
Some repositories ship a text model and an image model together, such as SigLIP2. FastEncodeMultimodal loads both from one repository and gives you encode_text and encode_image. The default, siglip2_so400m, reads images at 512 pixels and cuts text at 64 tokens.
Other models come as a matched pair in separate repositories. nomic-embed-text v1.5 and nomic-embed-vision v1.5 both produce 768-dimensional vectors in the same space, so load FastEncode(nomic_text_v15) and FastEncodeImage(nomic_vision_v15) separately and compare their vectors directly.

title: utils
text:
Embedding with no model
hash_embed makes vectors without any model or download, and gives the same vectors on every run and every machine. It lowercases each text, takes every run of 3 to 5 consecutive characters (character n-grams), hashes each run with CRC32 into one of 256 slots, counts the hits per slot, and scales the result to length 1. Two texts score high when they share many character runs, so the vectors measure spelling, not meaning: “rank fusion” is close to “rank fusions”, but “cat” and “feline” score near zero.
It has two uses. One is matching names, such as people or places, where shared spelling is most of the signal anyway. The other is an index built where no real encoder can be downloaded, for example in a sandbox without network access.

title: core
text:
This page covers the lower of litesearch’s two routes. database() opens a SQLite database ready for search, get_store creates a store in it, and Database.search runs a hybrid query against that store. The rest are the parts those three are made of, which you can also call on their own: keyword search, exact and approximate vector search, rank fusion, spelling correction and a few tools for writing from several threads.
A store is a table with one row per chunk of text. It has a content column for the text, an embedding column for the text’s vector, a metadata column for JSON, and an FTS5 full-text index over content and metadata that SQLite keeps up to date as rows change. If you do not need your own schema or SQL, [Index](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) sets all of this up for you.

title: core
text:
Stores
get_store creates a store, or opens it if it exists. By default the id column is an integer that SQLite assigns. With hash=True, id is a SHA-1 hash of the content instead, so inserting the same text twice leaves one row. That suits code and other text you re-ingest often. With ann=True, the store also gets an HNSW index for fast vector search, described below.
upsert_all writes rows with a single prepared statement per batch: rows whose primary key is new are inserted, and rows whose key already exists are updated.

A store records which encoder and which tokenizer created it, in a table called store_meta. Reopening it with a different one raises StoreMismatch.
The vectors from two encoders cannot be compared, even when they have the same length. potion-base-8M and potion-multilingual-128M both produce 256 numbers per text, so nothing about the vectors shows that they came from different models. Before this check, opening a store with the wrong encoder added vectors from another model to the same index, and searches returned wrong neighbours without any error. The tokenizer is recorded for the same reason: a query tokenized differently from the index looks for tokens the index does not contain. An encoder with no name records '', and an empty value never conflicts, because litesearch cannot tell what a custom encoder is.

reopen()                                                             # an unnamed encoder never conflicts
test_eq(db._store_meta('s')['encoder'], 'a/one')

title: core
section: Searching one leg at a time
text:
Searching one leg at a time
A hybrid search has two legs, a keyword search and a vector search. Each is available on its own, on any table, not only on stores.
fts_search runs an FTS5 query and returns rows ordered by bm25 rank. FTS5 reports bm25 as a negative number in the rank column, so lower is better.
vec_search is exact vector search. It computes the distance from the query vector to every row’s embedding in SQL and returns the nearest rows, with the distance in _dist. When usearch’s SQLite extension is off, it computes the same distances with numpy and returns the same rows; a where that names _dist works only in SQL. It reads every row, so it is always correct and gets slower as the table grows; up to a few thousand rows it is fast. ann_search, further down, is the approximate alternative for large stores.
Both legs take the vector’s number type as dtype, and getting it wrong is silent in SQL. model2vec encoders return float32 and FastEncode returns float16. If float32 bytes are searched as float16, the distance function reads them as twice as many float16 numbers, many of them invalid, and returns NULL for every row. The vector leg then comes back in table order, and a hybrid search quietly becomes a keyword search. _dtype_check warns when the dtype differs from the one the store’s HNSW index recorded, or when every distance comes back NULL or 0.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion
rrf_all merges ranked lists into one. Each row earns weight / (k + position) from every list it appears in, counting positions from 0, and the amounts add up. With the default k=60, the top row of a list earns 1/60 and the row at position 60 earns half that. A row that appears in two lists collects two amounts, so it usually beats a row that tops only one. Because RRF uses positions only, it can merge lists whose scores are not comparable, such as bm25 ranks and vector distances. Rows are matched across lists by id_key, rowid by default. weights gives each list more or less influence.

from litesearch.core import rrf_all, rrf_merge

fts = [dict(rowid=1, t='a'), dict(rowid=2, t='b'), dict(rowid=3, t='c')]
vec = [dict(rowid=3, t='c'), dict(rowid=4, t='d')]
